clue.text: Peaceful state of one river flowing into another

indicators.note: one river flowing into another is pictured as the first river's letter running inside the second river's name

parts.note: the Oder is a river of central Europe, along the German-Polish border
R is the standard abbreviation for river

explanation.surface: A geographical note on where one river joins another and the calm that follows.
explanation.walkthrough: 'flowing into' puts R inside ODER. 'Peaceful state' is the sense in 'law and order'.
explanation.definitionFit: Order is a state of calm and lawful quiet, as in 'restore order' after a riot.

clue.text: Tyrant imprisons crowd in appallingly poor surroundings

indicators.note: crowd in surroundings puts the crowd inside the other letters
poor surroundings are the letters that encircle the crowd
appallingly means the letters of poor are badly jumbled

parts.note: a press is a crowd, a crush of people

explanation.surface: A dictator locks up a mob in squalid conditions.
explanation.walkthrough: 'appallingly' rearranges the given word to OPOR. 'imprisons' adds colour only, since 'Tyrant' is the definition and the container is signalled by 'in ... surroundings'.
explanation.definitionFit: An oppressor rules harshly and cruelly, like a despot.

clue.text: He sounds like a powerful weight-lifter

indicators.note: sounds like tells us the next phrase gives a word that is only heard, not spelt

parts.note: a derrick is a crane for lifting heavy loads

explanation.surface: A man is said to resemble a strongman athlete.
explanation.walkthrough: 'weight-lifter' suggests an athlete; it is a crane. 'He' just means a man's name.
explanation.definitionFit: Derek is a male given name, so it can stand for any he.

clue.text: Opportunity to marry a fellow lodger

parts.note: room means scope or opportunity, as in room for improvement
to mate is an old word for to marry or pair off

explanation.surface: A chance to wed someone who shares the boarding house.
explanation.definitionFit: A roommate shares lodgings or a room with another person.

clue.text: Sharp rebuke for drummer before recommittal, say

indicators.note: drummer before recommittal places the salesman's word ahead of the other piece

parts.note: a drummer is an old US word for a travelling salesman, a rep

indicators.note: say tells us the following word is only approximately sounded, not spelt

parts.note: a remand is a recommittal of an accused person to custody

explanation.surface: Someone imagines a percussionist being sent back to prison and getting a telling-off.
explanation.walkthrough: 'say' marks REMAND as a sound-alike: spoken quickly it gives the RIMAND ending. 'drummer' is not a percussionist but an American travelling salesman (a rep).
explanation.definitionFit: A reprimand is a formal scolding or official reproof.

clue.text: Genuine old Spanish coin

definitions.meaning: a former silver coin of Spain

explanation.definitionFit: Real means authentic; the real was also a historic silver coin of Spain.

clue.text: Top courier disorientated in the Caribbean

indicators.note: a disorientated courier has lost his bearings, so the letters are mixed up

explanation.surface: A leading delivery driver gets lost somewhere in the West Indies.
explanation.definitionFit: Puerto Rico is an island territory of the United States lying in the West Indies.

clue.text: Transfix one member with whitish face

parts.note: I is the Roman numeral for one
M is an abbreviation for member, as in MBE
a pale face is whitish, so whitish face gives pale

explanation.surface: Someone skewers a ghostly-looking club member.
explanation.walkthrough: 'member' is the M of titles like MBE, not the usual MP.
explanation.definitionFit: To impale is to pierce through with a sharp stake or spear.

clue.text: Duck drinks, we hear, with unusual 19

indicators.note: we hear tells us the drinks word is heard rather than spelt

parts.note: ales are drinks of beer

indicators.note: unusual means the letters of the cross-referenced word are put in an odd order

parts.note: 19 across is RUBY

explanation.surface: A duck sips something, apparently, accompanied by a strange girl.
explanation.walkthrough: 'unusual' rearranges the answer to 19 across, giving BURY. Aylesbury, a town in Buckinghamshire, England, gave its name to a breed of white table duck.
explanation.definitionFit: The Aylesbury is a breed of large white domestic duck raised for the table.

clue.text: Theologian dined in, being old-fashioned

indicators.note: dined in places the eating word inside the theologian's letters

parts.note: DD, Doctor of Divinity, is a theologian's degree
ate means dined

explanation.surface: A divine stayed home for supper, showing his conservative habits.
explanation.walkthrough: 'dined in' looks like staying home; 'in' puts ATE into DD.
explanation.definitionFit: Dated means out of date, belonging to an earlier time.

clue.text: Crime concealed by attendant in the Brontës' dwelling

indicators.note: a crime concealed by an attendant is tucked inside the attendant's word

parts.note: a page is a boy attendant, as at a wedding or court
arson, deliberate fire-raising, is a crime

explanation.surface: A literary mystery: some crime hushed up by a servant at the Brontë family home.
explanation.walkthrough: The Brontë sisters grew up in Haworth Parsonage, Yorkshire, where their father was the vicar.
explanation.definitionFit: The Brontës lived in the vicarage house at Haworth, the clergyman's residence provided by the church.

clue.text: Smug group's conduct

parts.note: pi, short for pious, means sanctimonious or smug in British slang
a lot is a group or set, as in 'that lot'; the 's is a link

explanation.surface: Someone sniffs at the behaviour of a self-satisfied clique.
explanation.walkthrough: 'conduct' looks like a noun meaning behaviour; it is the verb meaning to guide or steer. PI is British school slang for pious.
explanation.definitionFit: To pilot something is to steer or guide it, as a pilot guides a ship into harbour.

clue.text: Language used by Kipling character in Orient (sic)

parts.note: the Orient is the East, abbreviated E

indicators.note: the character in sic places the boy's name inside the word for thus

parts.note: sic is Latin for thus, so
Kim is the boy hero of Rudyard Kipling's novel Kim

explanation.surface: A tongue spoken by one of Kipling's heroes in the East, with a scholarly sic attached.
explanation.walkthrough: '(sic)' looks like an editor's aside but is a piece of wordplay: sic means 'thus', SO.
explanation.definitionFit: Eskimo is the older collective name for the Inuit and Yupik languages of the Arctic.

clue.text: Idly sets new 1 ac, given a conventional form

indicators.note: 1 across is ORDER, so new 1 ac reads as new order, a rearrangement of the letters

explanation.surface: Someone lazily establishes a new regime and makes it conventional.
explanation.walkthrough: The anagram signal is a cross-reference: 1 across is ORDER, so 'new 1 ac' says 'new order' for IDLY SETS.
explanation.definitionFit: Something stylised is drawn or presented in a conventional, non-realistic manner, as in heraldic art.

clue.text: Appear again during land survey, making us red

indicators.note: during places the jumbled words in the middle of the survey word

parts.note: a recce, military slang for reconnaissance, is a survey of the land

indicators.note: making means the letters of us red are made into something new

explanation.surface: Surveyors working a field suddenly appear, and we blush.
explanation.walkthrough: 'making' rearranges US RED, and 'during' puts that inside the survey word. RECCE is British army slang for a reconnaissance; the definition is a rare verb used of diseases breaking out again.
explanation.definitionFit: To recrudesce is to break out again after a dormant spell, as a disease or unrest can.

clue.text: One loved by little girl? Right, in a way

indicators.note: Right, in a way places the little girl and R inside the road abbreviation

parts.note: St, street, is a way or road
wee is Scottish and informal for little
Thea is a girl's name

explanation.surface: A small girl's beloved, with a passing comment that this is right in a sense.
explanation.walkthrough: The comma tricks you into reading 'Right' as an exclamation; it is just R. The question mark admits a little girl's darling is only one kind of beloved.
explanation.definitionFit: A sweetheart is a beloved person, a darling or lover.

clue.text: Ready for action in conflict in the Med perhaps

indicators.note: conflict in the Med places the fighting word within the other letters
perhaps signals the letters of Med may be arranged otherwise

parts.note: a battle is a conflict

explanation.surface: Warships primed for combat in a Mediterranean war.
explanation.walkthrough: 'perhaps' rearranges the sea's abbreviation to EMD, and 'in' places the conflict between its second and third letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Embattled describes forces drawn up in battle array, prepared to fight.

clue.text: Escort loses prisoner in the Tube

indicators.note: escort loses prisoner means the convict's word is removed from the escorting word

parts.note: to conduct someone is to escort or lead them
con, a convict, is a prisoner

explanation.surface: A guard on the London Underground lets his prisoner slip away.
explanation.walkthrough: 'the Tube' suggests the London Underground; here it is just a pipe.
explanation.definitionFit: A duct is a pipe or channel carrying fluid or air.

clue.text: Note about row in news agency causes delay

indicators.note: in news agency places everything before it inside the agency's name

parts.note: Tass was the Soviet news agency

indicators.note: note about row puts the note's letters around the row

parts.note: re is the second note of the sol-fa scale
a din is a noisy row

explanation.surface: A musical note about a quarrel at the press bureau holds things up.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Note' is a sol-fa note; 'about' wraps it round the row, making RDINE, and 'in' sets that inside the Soviet agency's name.
explanation.definitionFit: Tardiness is lateness, slowness in arriving or acting.

clue.text: Knowing Mr Lear was so nice!

definitions.text: Knowing Mr Lear was so nice!

parts.words: Knowing Mr Lear was so nice!
parts.note: a nod to the self-mocking Edward Lear poem whose title and refrain say how agreeable it is to know Mr Lear

explanation.walkthrough: Edward Lear, Victorian nonsense poet, wrote a comic self-portrait whose refrain is 'How pleasant to know Mr Lear!'. The clue paraphrases it with 'nice' in place of the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Pleasant means agreeable or nice, the word in Lear's famous line.

clue.text: Girl drops fag-end in middle of game

indicators.note: drops tells us a letter is taken away from the sport's name

parts.note: rugby is a ball game

indicators.note: end of fag points to the final letter of that word, the one dropped from the game

explanation.surface: A girl puts out her cigarette in the middle of a match.
explanation.walkthrough: 'fag' is British slang for cigarette, so 'fag-end' looks like a stub; it is the letter G, which sits in the middle of RUGBY.
explanation.definitionFit: Ruby is a female given name.

clue.text: Good fellow worked early as a builder

parts.note: a brick is old British slang for a good, reliable person

indicators.note: worked means the letters of early are worked into a new shape

explanation.surface: A decent chap toiled from dawn as a construction worker.
explanation.walkthrough: 'You're a brick' is dated British praise for a dependable friend. 'worked' shuffles EARLY into LAYER.
explanation.definitionFit: A bricklayer is a tradesman who builds walls with bricks and mortar.

clue.text: One who does not return a ring

definitions.meaning: someone who holds on to things
a guard ring worn to stop another slipping off

explanation.definitionFit: A keeper keeps what he is given; a keeper is also a guard ring worn above a wedding ring.

clue.text: Beads scattered about the chapel

indicators.note: the shuffled beads sit about, that is around, the word the
beads scattered are strewn about, so their letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone's rosary beads are spilt all round the chapel floor.
explanation.walkthrough: 'scattered' rearranges the beads to BESDA, and 'about' wraps that round the article. Bethesda is a common name for Welsh nonconformist chapels.
explanation.definitionFit: Bethesda, from a biblical pool, names many Nonconformist meeting houses, especially in Wales.

clue.text: Trinket originally bought in Johannesburg or Uganda

indicators.note: originally points to the first letter of each of the following words

explanation.surface: A trinket first purchased in South Africa or East Africa.
explanation.definitionFit: A bijou is a small, dainty jewel or ornament.

clue.text: A large deer reversed it with one foot

indicators.note: reversed applies to the whole string it, one and foot, read backwards together

parts.note: I is the Roman numeral for one
a paw is an animal's foot

explanation.surface: A big stag backed up with one of its hooves.
explanation.walkthrough: 'A large deer' could be the start of the wordplay, but it is the whole definition; 'reversed' then turns ITIPAW round.
explanation.definitionFit: The wapiti is the North American elk, a very large red deer.

clue.text: Alphabetical list displayed in parts of a ship, it's said

indicators.note: it's said tells us the phrase is spoken, not spelt

parts.note: in gives IN; a ship's decks are its storeys, so parts of a ship are decks

explanation.surface: A listing posted on the various levels of a vessel, apparently.
explanation.walkthrough: 'displayed' is only a link; the joke is that 'in decks' and the answer sound the same.
explanation.definitionFit: An index is an alphabetical list of topics at the back of a book.

clue.text: A small price to pay for church writings

parts.note: CE is the Church of England
NT, the New Testament, is a body of sacred writings

explanation.surface: Paying a little for religious texts is a small sacrifice.
explanation.walkthrough: CE (Church of England) and NT (New Testament) are standard crossword abbreviations.
explanation.definitionFit: A cent is a coin worth one hundredth of a dollar, a trifling sum.

clue.text: Record month, at first, for sweet drink

indicators.note: month at first places the month ahead of the record

parts.note: Jul is the abbreviation for July
an EP, extended play, is a type of record

explanation.surface: A diary note: a record month, first, then a sweet drink to celebrate.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Record month' looks like a best-ever month; the words split, with the month placed first.
explanation.definitionFit: A julep is a sweet drink, now usually a mint julep of bourbon, sugar and mint.

clue.text: Disappear quickly when King Edward appears on horseback

indicators.note: King Edward appears on horseback, that is seated within the horse's seat word

parts.note: to be on horseback is to be in the saddle
K is the chess and card abbreviation for king
Ed is short for Edward

explanation.surface: Onlookers flee as soon as the mounted king rides into view.
explanation.walkthrough: 'appears on horseback' means sitting in the seat of a horse. 'King Edward' is also a British potato variety, a red herring.
explanation.definitionFit: To skedaddle is informal for running away hurriedly.

clue.text: Lying on the floor, it's not sufficiently appreciated

definitions.meaning: felt too little, read as a two-part phrase

explanation.definitionFit: Underfelt is the felt underlay beneath a carpet; split as under-felt it means felt too little, valued below its worth.

clue.text: Unknown ingredient in meals where LBJ was born

indicators.note: an unknown ingredient in meals sits inside the meals word

parts.note: teas are meals, as in high tea
x is the mathematical symbol for an unknown

explanation.surface: A mystery ingredient turns up in the food of Lyndon Johnson's birthplace.
explanation.walkthrough: LBJ is President Lyndon Baines Johnson, born near Stonewall. In Britain 'tea' can be an evening meal.
explanation.definitionFit: Lyndon B. Johnson, US president, was born in Stonewall, a town in the Lone Star State.
